objectives: LO 6.1.1: Recognize risk-and-return terms used in building and managing portfolios (diversification, asset allocation, expected return)
LO 6.1.2: Separate systematic (PRIME) from unsystematic risks and identify each source
LO 6.2.1: Calculate beta and weighted portfolio beta and explain how they guide portfolio construction
LO 6.2.2: Calculate mean and standard deviation for one asset and the 1-, 2- and 3-SD return ranges
LO 6.2.3: Calculate the coefficient of variation and use it to compare risk per unit of return
LO 6.2.4: Use covariance and correlation to compute a two-asset portfolio's standard deviation
LO 6.2.5: Calculate R-squared and use it to judge whether beta is a reliable risk measure
synthesis: This module supplies the risk math the rest of investment planning runs on. Standard deviation and beta feed the Sharpe, Treynor and Jensen performance measures and CAPM-style required returns; correlation and covariance drive asset allocation and modern portfolio theory; and R-squared tells you which of those risk measures you can trust. In client work, these numbers turn "how risky is this?" into ranges, comparisons and diversification choices a client can see.

example.title: Is the new fund a real diversifier?
example.html:
Rosa holds an S&P 500 index fund. A candidate fund has σ = 20, the market σ = 16, and their covariance is 224.

  1. ρ = 224 ÷ (20 × 16) = 0.70
  2. R2 = 0.702 = 0.49 → under 0.70, so it is not just an index look-alike, and beta (224 ÷ 256 = 0.875) is not reliable
  3. Judge it with standard deviation and Sharpe, and check portfolio SD: at 50/50 with this correlation, √[0.25(400) + 0.25(256) + 2(0.25)(224)] = √276 ≈ 16.61, below the 18.00 weighted-average SD.

keyNumbers: Share of returns within ±1, 2, 3 SD (textbook uses 99%, not 99.7%)
Large-cap stocks in different industries to diversify (exam rule)
Small/mid-cap stocks / mutual funds in different asset classes
Sample SD divisor for historical returns (calculator S<sub>x</sub>)
Only case where portfolio SD = weighted-average SD
mustKnow: Total risk (SD) = systematic (beta) + unsystematic; PRIME = purchasing power, reinvestment rate, interest rate, market, exchange rate
COV = ρσ<sub>i</sub>σ<sub>j</sub>; ρ = COV ÷ (σ<sub>i</sub>σ<sub>j</sub>); R<sup>2</sup> = ρ<sup>2</sup>; 1 − R<sup>2</sup> = unsystematic share
Normal distribution for annual returns; lognormal for ending portfolio value
traps: Low beta ≠ low volatility — low correlation shrinks beta (gold funds)
Liquidity and marketability risk are unsystematic; common stock has no default risk
Don't weight-average SDs unless ρ = +1; don't stop at the variance
Only one tail: 95% within ±2 SD leaves 2.5% above and 2.5% below
CV questions pad the facts — ignore beta and R<sup>2</sup>
tips: Check R<sup>2</sup> first: it tells you whether to trust beta (Treynor/Jensen) or use SD (Sharpe)
Correlation pyramid: covariance (unbounded) → correlation (−1 to +1) → R<sup>2</sup> (square it)
Zero-coupon bonds eliminate reinvestment rate risk; Yankee bonds reduce exchange rate risk
